title: The Street Era
bigQuestion: How did videotape, smaller boards and city streets change what skateboarding looked like in the 1990s?

story.title: A Copy of a Copy
story.kicker: A worn videotape travels around a small town and changes how everyone skates.
paragraphs: It is the fall of 1991 in a small town far from California. Dana's cousin mails her a VHS tape. The label is handwritten. The picture is fuzzy, because this tape is a copy of a copy of a copy. Each time a tape is copied onto another, the image gets a little worse.

Dana and three friends crowd around a television in her basement. On the screen, skaters roll through city streets and school yards. One rides backward, then turns and pops off a curb. They rewind the same few seconds again and again. The rewind button gets a workout.

The next day the tape leaves Dana's house in a backpack. It goes to Marcus, then to the twins down the block, then to the kid who works at the bike and skate shop. By winter, almost every skater in town has watched it. At the bank parking lot after closing, people try to copy what they saw.

Nobody in town has seen these skaters in person. Nobody has a magazine that shows the whole trick. But the tape shows every step, start to finish, from feet to landing. Within a year, the kids in Dana's town skate in a new style. A box of plastic and magnetic tape taught them.
story.think: Why could a fuzzy home-copied videotape teach a trick better than a sharp photo in a magazine?

lessons.title: From Photos to Moving Pictures
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1980s, home video let skaters watch a whole trick from start to finish, so new tricks spread much faster than through photos alone.
reading: Before home video, most skaters learned new tricks from magazines. *Thrasher* began in 1981, and TransWorld SKATEboarding began in 1983. A photo froze one moment, often the highest point of a trick. A reader could see where the board was, but not how the feet got it there.

Home *VHS* players spread through American homes in the 1980s. In 1984, Powell Peralta released The Bones Brigade Video Show. Companies saw that a team video could sell boards and show off their riders. Skaters could watch a trick, rewind it, and watch it again in slow motion.

Tapes were also easy to copy. A skater with two VCRs could record a friend's tape onto a blank one. Copies traveled through mail, schools and skate shops. A trick filmed in California could reach a kid in Ohio or Ontario within months. Video became the main way tricks moved from place to place.

words.d: a skateboarding magazine started in 1981, known for covering street and backyard skating
a home videotape format of the 1980s and 1990s, played in a VCR
a film made by a skate company or crew to show its riders' tricks

look.cite: Publication and release years of each magazine and video

choices: every step of a trick from start to landing
the skater's name in large letters
a sharper image of one moment
check.why: A photo freezes one moment; video shows the whole trick and can be rewound and watched again.

check.q: Which company released The Bones Brigade Video Show in 1984?
check.why: Powell Peralta made The Bones Brigade Video Show in 1984 to show its team.

Copies were only allowed in California.

lessons.title: Video Days, 1991
lessons.mainIdea: Blind's Video Days (1991) showed loose, creative street skating and became one of the most copied skate videos ever made.
reading: In 1991, the skate company Blind released *Video Days*. Blind had been started by the street skater Mark Gonzales. The video was directed by Spike Jonze, who later became a well-known Hollywood film director. It is shorter than most movies, but skaters still talk about it decades later.

Video Days followed a small crew, including Mark Gonzales, Guy Mariano and Jason Lee. Jason Lee later became a film and television actor. Each skater had a *part*, a section of the video built around one rider, set to a song. The skating happened on streets, in parking lots and on school grounds, not on big ramps.

The style felt relaxed and playful. Riders rolled smoothly, linked tricks together and used whatever the city offered. Many viewers saw for the first time that a curb, a bench or a bank of concrete could be a whole skatepark. The video helped make street skating the center of the sport in the early 1990s.

words.d: a 1991 skate video by Blind, directed by Spike Jonze, famous for its street skating
a section of a skate video that features one skater, usually set to one song
skating on things found in a city, such as curbs, ledges, benches and banks

look.title: Watching a Part
look.text: Picture a skater's part in an early-1990s video. A song starts. The skater rolls down a sidewalk, pops onto a curb, slides along it and rolls away. The camera follows close behind, low to the ground. The next clip shows a different spot in a different city. Three minutes later the song ends, and so does the part.
look.prompt: Why might a skate company put one rider's best tricks together with one song?

check.q: Who directed Video Days?
check.why: Spike Jonze directed Video Days in 1991 and later directed Hollywood films.

check.q: Where was most of the skating in Video Days filmed?
choices: streets, parking lots and school grounds
check.why: Video Days showed street skating on things found around a city.

check.q: What is a skater's part in a video?
choices: a broken piece of the board
a section that features one skater, usually set to one song
check.why: A part is a section built around one rider and usually one song.

lessons.title: Questionable and the Video Race
lessons.mainIdea: After Questionable (1992), companies raced to make videos with harder tricks, and new video magazines spread the newest tricks even faster.
reading: In 1992, the company Plan B released *Questionable*. Its team included Rodney Mullen, Danny Way and Colin McKay. Mullen had already invented many flat-ground tricks in the 1980s. Questionable showed very technical street skating, with flip tricks linked into grinds and slides. It also showed skaters on large handrails and long sets of stairs.

Questionable raised the bar for what a pro had to do on film. Other companies answered with their own videos. Each new video tried to show tricks no one had filmed before. The word *technical* came to describe skating with many fast, precise flips and spins of the board.

Skaters also wanted news faster than a yearly team video. In 1993, 411 Video Magazine began sending out a new tape every few months. Each issue mixed clips from many companies, contests and cities. For a kid far from California, a new issue showed what was happening across the whole skate world.

words.d: a 1992 skate video by Plan B, known for very technical street skating
describes skating with many quick, precise flips and spins of the board
a trick in which the board spins under the skater's feet, such as a kickflip

look.title: Two Tapes Side by Side
look.text: Imagine two tapes on a shelf. One, from the mid-1980s, shows riders flying high above vert ramps. The other, from 1992, shows riders on the street flipping the board twice, landing on a ledge and sliding to the end. Both are hard. Each shows the kind of skating its time cared about most.
look.prompt: What changed in where skaters skated between the two tapes?

check.q: Which company released Questionable in 1992?
check.why: Plan B released Questionable in 1992.

check.q: What does technical mean when skaters describe a style?
choices: skating with many quick, precise flips and spins of the board
check.why: Technical skating uses many fast, precise flip tricks and combinations.

check.q: What did 411 Video Magazine add starting in 1993?
choices: a new tape every few months with clips from many companies
the first skate magazine in print
check.why: 411 Video Magazine sent out regular tapes that mixed clips from many companies and places.

sections.title: A New Board for the Street

lessons.title: Small Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: Street skaters in the early 1990s chose small, hard wheels because they made boards lighter and lower for flip tricks, even though they rolled worse over cracks.
reading: Many 1980s boards rolled on wheels about 60 millimeters or more across. Those wheels were made for ramps and pools. In the early 1990s, street skaters shrank their wheels. Some rode wheels around 40 millimeters across, much smaller than a wheel today. Wheel size is the *diameter*, the distance straight across the wheel through its center.

Small wheels did three things. They made the whole board lighter, so it was easier to flip. They put the deck closer to the ground, so the board had less distance to travel when it popped. They also let the skater feel the board land under the feet. For flip tricks on flat ground, that helped.

Small wheels also had problems, and physics explains them. A small wheel meets the edge of a crack or pebble at a steeper angle, so more of its forward motion is stopped. Riders got tossed by tiny bumps. Small, hard wheels also wore *flat spots* faster when a skater skidded. By the late 1990s, many skaters moved back toward medium sizes, around the low 50s.

words.d: the distance straight across a circle through its center; for wheels, given in millimeters
flat places worn into a wheel by skidding, which make the ride bumpy
a scale for hardness; skate wheels use the A scale, from about 78A (soft) to about 101A (hard)

look.title: Wheel Sizes Over Time
look.cite: Example sizes in typical ranges; wheel makers print diameter in millimeters
look.prompt: About how many millimeters smaller is the early-1990s example than the 1980s example?

check.q: Why did small wheels help flip tricks on flat ground?
choices: They made the board lighter and lower.
They were softer than older wheels.
check.why: Smaller wheels cut weight and lowered the deck, so the board flipped and popped more easily.

check.q: Why does a small wheel get stopped more easily by a crack?
choices: It meets the crack's edge at a steeper angle.
It spins faster than a large wheel.
check.why: A small wheel hits the edge of a bump more head-on, so more of its forward motion is blocked.

check.q: What is a wheel's diameter?
choices: the distance straight across the wheel through its center
check.why: Diameter is the distance across a circle through its center, measured in millimeters for wheels.

lessons.title: The Double-Kick Deck
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1990s, decks became narrower with a nose and a tail of almost the same shape, so skaters could do tricks rolling either direction.
reading: A 1980s deck often looked like a fish or a wide paddle. It had a big kicked-up tail and a short, small nose. Those boards worked well on ramps and in pools, where riders mostly used the tail. On the street, though, skaters began doing tricks off the front of the board as well as the back.

By the early 1990s, most street decks had a *double kick*: a nose and a tail turned up at about the same angle. The outline looked like a popsicle stick, so people called it the *popsicle shape*. Decks also grew narrower. A narrow, even board was lighter and easier to flip with the feet.

The new shape changed the tricks. With a real nose, a skater could pop off the front of the board. That move is the *nollie*, short for nose ollie. A double-kick board also rides the same in either direction, which made switch and fakie tricks easier. Almost every street deck sold today still uses this shape.

words.d: a deck with both the nose and the tail turned up, at about the same angle
the rounded, even outline of a modern double-kick street deck
an ollie popped off the nose of the board instead of the tail

look.title: Two Decks on the Floor
look.text: Lay two decks on the floor. The first is wide, with a long kicked tail and a short, flat nose. The second is narrower, and its nose and tail curve up almost the same. Turn the second board around and it looks nearly the same. Turn the first around and the difference is obvious.
look.prompt: Which deck would be easier to ride in both directions, and why?

check.q: What is a double-kick deck?
choices: a deck with two sets of trucks
a deck with a nose and a tail turned up at about the same angle
a deck made of two layers
a deck that is twice as long
check.why: A double kick means both ends turn up, at about the same angle.

check.q: What is a nollie?
choices: an ollie popped off the tail
a slide on the middle of the deck
an ollie popped off the nose
a turn on the back wheels
check.why: Nollie is short for nose ollie: the pop comes from the nose.

check.q: Why did the popsicle shape help switch and fakie tricks?
choices: The board rides about the same in either direction.
It was heavier, so it felt steadier.
It had no nose at all.
check.why: With matching ends, the board behaves the same whichever way it rolls.

lessons.title: Riding Fakie and Switch
lessons.mainIdea: Fakie means rolling backward in your normal stance, and switch means riding with your other foot in front; street skaters of the 1990s used both.
reading: Every skater has a usual stance. *Regular* skaters ride with the left foot in front, and *goofy* skaters ride with the right foot in front. Both are normal. Riding *fakie* means keeping your usual stance but rolling backward, toward your back foot. Riding *switch* means standing the opposite way, with your usual back foot in front.

You can learn to roll fakie on flat ground once you can push and stop well. Wear a buckled helmet and wrist guards, and pick a smooth, empty spot. First, roll forward slowly with both feet over the bolts. Next, stop, then gently push off a wall or a friend's hand so the board rolls backward. Keep your knees bent and your weight centered between the trucks. Look over your back shoulder at where you are going.

A common problem is leaning too far toward the nose, which makes the board shoot out. The fix is to keep your shoulders lined up over the board and stay low. Switch feels strange at first, like writing with your other hand. In the 1990s, street pros learned whole sets of tricks switch and fakie, which doubled the number of tricks they could do.

words.d: a stance with the left foot in front
a stance with the right foot in front
rolling backward while standing in your usual stance
riding with your usual back foot in front, the opposite of your normal stance

look.title: Same Feet, New Direction
look.text: Stand on a board on the grass in your usual stance. Point to where the board would go forward. Now point the other way. If the board rolled that way with your feet unchanged, you would be riding fakie. Now swap: put your usual back foot in front. That is switch.
look.prompt: On the grass, which feels stranger to you, fakie or switch, and why?

check.q: What does riding fakie mean?
choices: riding with your other foot in front
rolling backward in your usual stance
riding on only the back wheels
check.why: Fakie keeps your usual stance but the board rolls backward.

check.q: When learning to roll fakie, where should your weight be?
choices: centered between the trucks with knees bent
on the tail so the nose lifts
check.why: Centered weight and bent knees keep the board from shooting out.

check.q: A goofy skater riding switch has which foot in front?
choices: whichever foot is closer to the nose at the start
check.why: Goofy is right foot forward, so switch for a goofy skater is left foot forward.

lessons.title: Ledges, Curbs and Plazas
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1990s, concrete ledges, curbs and open plazas became the main spots for street skating, and plazas like the Embarcadero in San Francisco became famous on film.
reading: Street skaters looked at cities differently. A low concrete *ledge* beside a planter, a long curb or a set of marble benches became something to grind or slide on. A *grind* is when the metal trucks scrape along an edge. A *slide* is when the wooden deck itself moves along the edge.

Skaters rubbed *wax* on edges so the trucks and deck would slide farther. Wax lowers the friction between the metal or wood and the concrete. Friction is the force that pushes back against something sliding. Less friction meant a longer grind before the board slowed and stopped.

Wide open plazas drew crowds of skaters. In the early 1990s, the Embarcadero plaza on San Francisco's waterfront became one of the most filmed spots in the world. Skaters met there daily, and videos showed its ledges and gaps again and again. City rules and redesigns later pushed skaters out, a pattern that repeated in many cities.

words.d: a raised concrete or stone edge that skaters grind or slide on
a trick in which the metal trucks scrape along an edge
a trick in which the wooden deck moves along an edge
a waxy block rubbed on edges to lower friction so the board slides farther

look.title: Reading a Plaza
look.text: Picture a city plaza on a Sunday. There is a long knee-high ledge along a planter, a short three-step set of stairs, a smooth brick floor and a low curb by the fountain. A street skater walks through it slowly, touching each edge, checking how smooth it is and where people walk.
look.prompt: Which feature in this plaza would be the safest for a beginner to practice a first grind on, and why?

check.q: What is the difference between a grind and a slide?
choices: A grind is on grass and a slide is on concrete.
A grind uses only the wheels; a slide uses the bearings.
In a grind the trucks scrape the edge; in a slide the deck moves along it.
check.why: Grinds use the metal trucks; slides use the wood of the deck.

check.q: Why do skaters rub wax on a ledge?
choices: to lower friction so the board slides farther
check.why: Wax lowers friction, so the board slows down less while grinding or sliding.

check.q: Which San Francisco plaza became one of the most filmed street spots in the early 1990s?
check.why: The Embarcadero plaza on San Francisco's waterfront was a famous early-1990s street spot.

lessons.title: Rails and Stairs on Film
lessons.mainIdea: Handrails and stairs became symbols of 1990s street skating on film, but they are pro-level and dangerous; learners practice on low flat bars and curbs at a skatepark.
reading: In the mid-1980s, Mark Gonzales was filmed and photographed sliding down handrails, and he is often credited with some of the first handrail tricks. By the early 1990s, videos such as Questionable showed pros sliding long rails and jumping down big sets of stairs. A *handrail* is a metal rail built for people to hold on stairs. A *stair set* is a group of steps skaters count, such as a five-stair.

These clips look smooth because they show the one try that worked. Pros often took dozens of tries and many hard falls to film one. A fall from a rail adds the height of the stairs to the fall. Stairs, handrails and gaps on public property are not places to learn. They also put skaters near walkers and cars.

Learners start low and build up. At a skatepark, a *flat bar* is a metal rail a few inches off the ground, and a painted curb is even lower. Wear a buckled helmet, wrist guards and pads. Practice the move on a low bar until it feels easy before ever thinking about anything higher. If a move feels scary, break it into smaller pieces, such as rolling beside the bar first.

words.d: a metal rail built beside stairs for people to hold
a group of steps that skaters count, such as a five-stair
a low, level metal rail at a skatepark, used to learn grinds and slides

look.title: One Clip, Many Tries
look.text: Picture a filming day in 1993. A pro tries a slide down a long rail. Try one: the board slips out. Try two: a hard fall on the hip. Tries three to fourteen: misses, scrapes and rests. Try fifteen lands, and it becomes three seconds of a video part. Viewers see only that one landing.
look.prompt: How might seeing only the landed try change what a viewer thinks a trick takes?

check.q: Who is often credited with some of the first handrail tricks in the mid-1980s?
check.why: Mark Gonzales is often credited with early handrail tricks in the mid-1980s.

check.q: Where should a learner practice a first grind?
choices: on a low flat bar or painted curb at a skatepark
on a curb next to traffic
check.why: A low flat bar or curb at a skatepark keeps falls small and away from cars and walkers.

check.q: Why do rail clips in videos make tricks look easier than they are?
choices: Videos are always in slow motion.
Rails in videos are made of rubber.
They show the one try that worked, not the many misses.
check.why: A video shows the landed try; the many failed tries and falls are left out.

lessons.title: The Skate Shop as Home Base
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1990s, local skate shops were community centers where skaters bought gear, watched new videos, found local spots and joined shop teams.
reading: In many towns, the local *skate shop* was the center of skating. It sold decks, trucks, wheels and shoes. It also held things a skater could not buy at a big store: advice, the newest magazines and a television playing the latest video. Before the internet, the shop was often the only place to learn what was new.

Shop workers were usually skaters themselves. They set up boards, tightened trucks and told new riders which wheels fit their spots. Many shops sponsored a *shop team*, a group of local skaters who got discounts or free gear and represented the shop at contests. For a young skater, making the shop team was a first step toward being noticed.

Shops also gathered people. A new video might have a *premiere*, a first showing at the shop, with the whole local scene crowded in. Shops organized small contests in parking lots and lobbied city councils for skateparks. They gave skaters, often treated as a problem on the street, a place where they belonged.

words.d: a store run by skaters that sells skate gear and often serves as a local gathering place
a group of local skaters supported by a shop with gear or discounts
the first public showing of a new video

look.title: A Saturday at the Shop
look.text: It is a Saturday in 1995. Behind the counter, a worker sets up a new board, pressing in bearings and tightening the trucks. A television in the corner plays the newest tape. Two kids ask where the smooth ledges are. A flyer on the door announces a parking-lot contest next weekend.
look.prompt: Name three things this shop gives skaters besides gear.

check.q: What is a shop team?
choices: a group of local skaters supported by a shop
check.why: A shop team is made of local skaters who get gear or discounts and represent the shop.

check.q: Before the internet, why was the skate shop important for news?
choices: It had the newest magazines and videos.
It made all the boards itself.
check.why: Shops carried new magazines and played new videos, often the only place in town to see them.

check.q: What is a video premiere at a skate shop?
choices: a contest for the best video
the last copy of a video
a video made by the shop's owner
the first showing of a new video
check.why: A premiere is a first public showing, often with the local scene crowded in.

lessons.title: Bans and a Slogan
lessons.mainIdea: As street skating grew, many cities banned skateboarding in downtowns and plazas, and skaters answered with the slogan Skateboarding Is Not a Crime.
reading: Street skating used public and private spaces built for other things. Owners worried about chipped ledges, noise and people getting hurt. Many cities passed *bans*, laws or rules saying no skateboarding in certain places. Signs reading No Skateboarding went up on plazas, schools and shopping centers. Skaters could be fined or have boards taken.

Skaters answered with a short *slogan*: Skateboarding Is Not a Crime. It appeared on stickers, shirts and board graphics through the 1980s and 1990s. The slogan argued that skating was a healthy activity, not a danger to the public. It also pointed out that many towns had banned street skating without building anywhere else to go.

Philadelphia's LOVE Park shows the pattern. Through the 1990s, its smooth granite ledges made it one of the most famous street spots in the world. In the early 2000s the city enforced a ban on skating there, despite protests. The plaza was later rebuilt. Fights like this led many cities to build public skateparks instead.

words.d: laws or rules that forbid an activity in certain places
a short, catchy phrase that sums up an idea or a cause
places open to everyone, such as plazas, parks and sidewalks

look.title: Two Sides of a Plaza
look.text: Picture a city meeting. A building manager says skaters chip the granite benches and startle office workers. A sixteen-year-old skater says there is no skatepark within ten miles, and the plaza is the only smooth place in town. Both are telling the truth about what they see.
look.prompt: What is one solution that could answer both the manager and the skater?

choices: Skating was a healthy activity, not a danger to the public.
Only pros should be allowed to skate.
check.why: The slogan pushed back against bans by calling skating healthy and harmless.

check.q: What made LOVE Park in Philadelphia famous with skaters?
check.why: LOVE Park's smooth granite ledges made it a famous 1990s street spot.

check.q: Why did property owners often ask for skating bans?
choices: They worried about chipped ledges, noise and injuries.
check.why: Owners worried about damage, noise and people getting hurt.

lessons.title: Gonzales and Kaupas
lessons.mainIdea: Mark Gonzales and Natas Kaupas helped invent modern street skating in the 1980s by treating walls, benches, rails and even fire hydrants as things to skate.
reading: In the 1980s, most famous skaters rode vert ramps and pools. Two young Californians helped change that. *Natas Kaupas* grew up skating the streets of Santa Monica. He rode up walls, ollied onto benches and was filmed spinning on top of a fire hydrant. Each of these showed that ordinary city objects could be skated.

*Mark Gonzales*, nicknamed the Gonz, rode with a loose, imaginative style. He tried tricks no one had named yet, and he is often credited with early handrail slides. He later started the company Blind, which made Video Days. Gonzales is also a painter and writer whose art has been shown in galleries.

Both skaters built *style*: the personal way a skater moves, beyond whether the trick lands. Skaters often say style matters as much as difficulty. Gonzales and Kaupas showed that creativity, seeing a new use for a wall or curb, could change the whole sport. The street era of the 1990s grew from what they started.

words.d: a Santa Monica street skater of the 1980s known for wallrides and skating city objects
a street skating pioneer nicknamed the Gonz who founded Blind and is also an artist
the personal way a skater moves and looks while doing tricks

look.title: Seeing the Street New
look.text: Walk down a city block in your mind. There is a bench, a low wall, a fire hydrant and a curb. A shopper sees places to sit and things to walk around. Natas Kaupas or Mark Gonzales in 1986 might have seen four new tricks. The block did not change. The way of seeing it did.
look.prompt: Why is seeing a new use for an ordinary object a kind of invention?
